nifty.short: India's benchmark stock index: the 50 largest NSE-listed companies.
nifty.long: The NIFTY 50 tracks 50 large, liquid companies listed on the National Stock Exchange (NSE), weighted by free-float market value. This app predicts its moves and trades options on it. One point of NIFTY is worth ₹65 per lot of NIFTY options.

nifty 50.short: India's benchmark stock index: the 50 largest NSE-listed companies.
nifty 50.long: The NIFTY 50 tracks 50 large, liquid companies listed on the National Stock Exchange (NSE), weighted by free-float market value. Its options are the most traded index options in the world.

bank nifty.short: NSE index of the 12 most liquid banking stocks.
bank nifty.long: Bank Nifty tracks India's large banks such as HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank. Banks are about a third of the NIFTY 50, so a strong Bank Nifty move usually drags NIFTY with it.

india vix.short: NSE's fear gauge: how much NIFTY movement options are pricing for the next 30 days.
india vix.long: India VIX is computed from NIFTY option prices and is quoted as an annualised percentage. Around 11–14 is calm; above 20 means traders expect big swings. Higher VIX makes options more expensive. Dividing VIX by about 16 gives a rough expected one-day move in percent.

vix.short: Volatility index; here usually India VIX, the market's expected volatility.
vix.long: A volatility index measures how much movement option prices imply over the next 30 days. India VIX is NIFTY's version; the US VIX is the S&P 500's. Rising VIX usually comes with falling stocks.

option.short: A contract giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at a fixed price before expiry.
option.long: The buyer pays a premium for the right; the seller receives it and takes on the obligation. NIFTY options are cash-settled: nobody delivers the index, the difference is paid in cash. Buyers can lose at most the premium they paid.

call option.short: An option that gains value when the underlying goes up (CE).
call option.long: A call gives the right to buy at the strike price. If NIFTY ends above the strike plus the premium you paid, the trade is profitable at expiry. On NSE calls are labelled CE (European style call).

ce.short: Call option (Call European). Profits when NIFTY rises.
ce.long: CE is NSE's label for a call option. Buying a CE is a bullish bet: it gains when NIFTY rises and loses value as time passes or if NIFTY falls. The most you can lose when buying is the premium.

put option.short: An option that gains value when the underlying goes down (PE).
put option.long: A put gives the right to sell at the strike price. Buying a put is a bearish bet or a hedge for a portfolio. On NSE puts are labelled PE (European style put).

pe.short: Put option (Put European). Profits when NIFTY falls.
pe.long: PE is NSE's label for a put option. Buying a PE is a bearish bet: it gains when NIFTY falls. Like any bought option it loses value every day through time decay.

strike.short: The fixed price at which an option can be exercised.
strike.long: NIFTY strikes are spaced 50 points apart (for example 23,800 and 23,850). Whether an option is in, at or out of the money depends on where NIFTY is relative to its strike.

strike price.short: The fixed price at which an option can be exercised.
strike price.long: NIFTY strikes are spaced 50 points apart. A call is worth something at expiry only if NIFTY is above its strike; a put only if NIFTY is below.

expiry.short: The date an option contract ends and is settled.
expiry.long: NIFTY has weekly options expiring every Tuesday (Thursday before September 2025) and monthly ones on the last Tuesday. After expiry an option is worth only its intrinsic value; all time value is gone.

weekly expiry.short: The NIFTY option contract that ends this week (Tuesday).
weekly expiry.long: Weekly options are cheap because they have little time left, which is why they are popular. They also lose value fastest, especially in the last two days. This app trades the nearest weekly expiry with at least one day left.

0dte.short: Zero days to expiry: trading an option on its expiry day.
0dte.long: On expiry day, options can double or go to zero within minutes because gamma is extreme and time value collapses. It is the riskiest day to trade options.

premium.short: The price of an option, quoted per unit.
premium.long: You pay premium × lot size to buy one lot. For example a premium of ₹140 on a 65-unit lot costs ₹9,100. Premium = intrinsic value + time value.

lot.short: The fixed contract size; NIFTY options trade in lots of 65 units.
lot.long: You cannot buy one unit of a NIFTY option, only whole lots. With lot size 65, a 1-point move in the premium changes your P&L by ₹65 per lot. NSE revises lot sizes periodically.

lot size.short: Units per contract: 65 for NIFTY (from the January 2026 series).
lot size.long: P&L in rupees = change in premium × lot size × number of lots. A ₹5,000 profit on one NIFTY lot needs the premium to rise by about 77 points.

atm.short: At the money: strike closest to the current NIFTY level.
atm.long: ATM options have the most time value and a delta near 0.5, so they move about half as much as NIFTY. They need the least capital among options that still react meaningfully to the index. This app's rules book buys the ATM call or put.

itm.short: In the money: an option that already has intrinsic value.
itm.long: A call is ITM when its strike is below NIFTY; a put when its strike is above. ITM options cost more but move more closely with NIFTY and lose less to time decay.

otm.short: Out of the money: an option with no intrinsic value yet.
otm.long: A call is OTM when its strike is above NIFTY; a put when its strike is below. OTM options are cheap but most expire worthless; they need a large move to pay off.

moneyness.short: Where the strike sits relative to the current price: ITM, ATM or OTM.
moneyness.long: Moneyness decides how an option behaves. Deep ITM options act like the index itself, ATM options are most sensitive to time and volatility, and far OTM options behave like lottery tickets.

intrinsic value.short: What an option would be worth if it expired right now.
intrinsic value.long: For a call it is NIFTY minus the strike (if positive); for a put it is the strike minus NIFTY. An OTM option has zero intrinsic value: its whole price is time value.

time value.short: The part of the premium paid for the chance of further movement.
time value.long: Time value shrinks every day and is zero at expiry. It is larger when volatility is high and when more time is left. Buyers pay it, sellers collect it.

ltp.short: Last traded price: the most recent price at which a trade happened.
ltp.long: LTP can be stale for illiquid strikes. For realistic paper fills this app prefers the live bid (when selling) or ask (when buying) over the LTP.

bid.short: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay.
bid.long: When you sell, you usually get the bid. The gap between bid and ask is a cost you pay on every round trip.

ask.short: The lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept.
ask.long: When you buy, you usually pay the ask. Liquid ATM NIFTY options have spreads of a fraction of a point; far OTM strikes can be much wider.

bid-ask spread.short: The gap between the best buy and sell prices.
bid-ask spread.long: You pay roughly half the spread when entering and half when exiting. On frequent trades it adds up, so the engine includes it in every backtest and paper fill.

option chain.short: A table of every strike's call and put prices, OI and IV for one expiry.
option chain.long: Traders read the chain to see where positions are concentrated (open interest), how expensive options are (IV) and where support or resistance may sit. Live chain data needs an Upstox token in this app.

delta.short: How much the option price moves for a 1-point move in NIFTY.
delta.long: ATM options have delta about 0.5 (calls) or −0.5 (puts); deep ITM options approach 1; far OTM approach 0. If NIFTY rises 100 points, an ATM call gains roughly 50 points of premium.

gamma.short: How fast delta changes as NIFTY moves.
gamma.long: High gamma means the option's sensitivity changes quickly. Gamma is highest for ATM options near expiry, which is why expiry-day premiums swing so violently.

theta.short: Value an option loses per day from the passage of time.
theta.long: Theta is negative for buyers and positive for sellers. It accelerates in the last 2–3 days before expiry. A bought option that sits still loses money because of theta.

vega.short: Change in premium for a 1-point change in implied volatility.
vega.long: Buyers gain when IV rises and lose when it falls. After events like RBI policy or results, IV often collapses (IV crush), so a correct direction call can still lose money.

iv.short: Implied volatility: the volatility priced into an option, as an annual %.
iv.long: IV is backed out from the option's market price. Higher IV means more expensive options. Comparing IV with the volatility that actually happens tells you whether options are cheap or rich.

implied volatility.short: The volatility priced into an option, as an annual %.
implied volatility.long: IV reflects how much movement the market expects. India VIX is essentially NIFTY's 30-day implied volatility. IV usually rises when markets fall.

iv crush.short: A sharp fall in implied volatility after an expected event passes.
iv crush.long: Before scheduled events (RBI, Budget, results) traders bid up option prices; once the news is out, IV drops and premiums fall even if the index moved in your direction.

atm iv.short: Implied volatility of the at-the-money option.
atm iv.long: ATM IV is the cleanest single read of how expensive options are for the current expiry. Compare it with India VIX and recent realised volatility.

oi.short: Open interest: number of option contracts currently open (not yet closed).
oi.long: Rising OI with rising prices suggests new positions are being built; falling OI suggests positions are being closed. Large OI at a strike often acts like a magnet or a wall.

open interest.short: Number of contracts currently open (not yet closed or expired).
open interest.long: Open interest counts outstanding positions, not trades. Option sellers typically hold the big OI, so heavy call OI above the market is often read as resistance and heavy put OI below as support.

pcr.short: Put-call ratio: total put OI divided by total call OI.
pcr.long: PCR above about 1.2 is often read as put writers supporting the market (bullish); below about 0.7 as call writers capping it (bearish). Extreme readings can also be contrarian signals. On its own it is a weak predictor.

max pain.short: The strike at which option buyers would lose the most at expiry.
max pain.long: Max pain is where the total value of all options expiring would be smallest. Some traders believe expiry tends to drift toward it; the evidence is weak, so treat it as context only.

call wall.short: The strike with the largest call open interest, often seen as resistance.
call wall.long: Call writers at that strike profit if NIFTY stays below it and may hedge in ways that slow a rally there. A break above the call wall can trigger short covering and a sharp move up.

put wall.short: The strike with the largest put open interest, often seen as support.
put wall.long: Put writers at that strike profit if NIFTY stays above it. A break below the put wall can accelerate selling as writers hedge or exit.

gex.short: Gamma exposure: estimated hedging pressure of option dealers, in ₹ crore.
gex.long: Positive GEX means dealers hedge against moves (they buy dips and sell rallies), which tends to calm the market. Negative GEX means their hedging amplifies moves. It is an estimate based on assumptions about who is long and short.

zero gamma.short: The NIFTY level where estimated dealer gamma flips from positive to negative.
zero gamma.long: Above the zero-gamma level markets often behave calmly; below it moves can speed up. It is a model estimate from the option chain, not an exact level.

rr25.short: 25-delta risk reversal: call IV minus put IV at 25 delta.
rr25.long: A negative RR25 means puts are more expensive than calls, i.e. traders pay up for crash protection. Very negative readings signal fear; moves toward zero signal complacency.

risk reversal.short: Difference between call and put implied volatility at the same delta.
risk reversal.long: It measures skew: which side the market is more worried about. In equity indices puts are usually richer, so the risk reversal is normally negative.

skew.short: Puts and calls at different strikes trade at different implied volatilities.
skew.long: Index puts usually carry higher IV than calls because investors buy protection. A steepening skew is a sign of rising fear.

implied move.short: The move (in %) the option market expects by expiry.
implied move.long: Roughly the price of the ATM straddle divided by NIFTY. If the implied move is 0.6%, the market prices about a two-in-three chance that NIFTY stays within ±0.6% by expiry.

straddle.short: Buying (or selling) the ATM call and put together.
straddle.long: A long straddle profits from a big move in either direction; a short straddle profits if NIFTY stays still. Its price is a direct read of the expected move.

iron condor.short: Sell an OTM call spread and an OTM put spread: profits if NIFTY stays in a range.
iron condor.long: The maximum profit is the credit received; the maximum loss is capped by the bought wings. It works in calm markets and loses in big moves.

credit spread.short: Sell one option and buy a further one: you receive money up front.
credit spread.long: A credit spread profits if NIFTY does not cross the sold strike. The bought option caps the loss, so the margin needed is far lower than selling naked.

debit spread.short: Buy one option and sell a further one to cut the cost.
debit spread.long: A debit spread is a cheaper directional bet with capped profit. It loses less to time decay than a single bought option.

hedge.short: A position that offsets the risk of another position.
hedge.long: Buying a put protects a portfolio from a fall; buying a far option caps the loss of a sold option. Hedges cost money but turn unlimited risk into known risk.

vrp.short: Volatility risk premium: implied volatility minus the volatility that actually happens.
vrp.long: Options are usually priced a bit higher than the movement that follows, which is why option sellers earn money on average. When VRP is positive, options look expensive relative to the volatility forecast.

har-rv.short: A standard model forecasting realised volatility from daily, weekly and monthly volatility.
har-rv.long: HAR-RV (heterogeneous autoregressive realised volatility) blends short and long volatility memories. The engine compares its forecast with India VIX to judge whether options are cheap or expensive.

realized volatility.short: How much NIFTY actually moved, measured from past prices.
realized volatility.long: Realised volatility is computed from returns over a window (for example the day's 5-minute bars). Comparing it with implied volatility tells you whether option prices were fair.

regime.short: The market's current state: calm or volatile, trending or ranging.
regime.long: Strategies behave differently by regime. Option buying tends to work in volatile trending markets, option selling in calm ranging ones. The engine tags the regime from volatility.

ohlc.short: Open, high, low and close prices of a time bar.
ohlc.long: Each bar (for example one minute or five minutes) records the first, highest, lowest and last price. Candles draw these four numbers.

candle.short: A bar drawn from open, high, low and close.
candle.long: The body spans open to close and is coloured by direction; the thin wicks show the high and low. A long wick shows prices were rejected at that level.

vwap.short: Volume-weighted average price for the day.
vwap.long: Institutions use VWAP as a benchmark: price above VWAP suggests buyers are in control. NIFTY spot has no volume of its own, so this app uses TWAP for the index.

twap.short: Time-weighted average price: the plain average of prices over the session.
twap.long: TWAP is used instead of VWAP for the NIFTY index, which has no traded volume. Distance from TWAP shows whether the current price is stretched relative to the day so far.

orb.short: Opening range breakout: a move beyond the first 30 minutes' high or low.
orb.long: The opening range is the high and low from 09:15 to 09:45. A break above or below it is a classic intraday momentum signal; it fails often in choppy markets.

cpr.short: Central pivot range: a band computed from yesterday's high, low and close.
cpr.long: A narrow CPR often precedes a trending day; a wide one a sideways day. Trading above the CPR is read as bullish, below it as bearish.

pivot.short: Support and resistance levels computed from the previous day's prices.
pivot.long: Pivot = (high + low + close) ÷ 3, with R1/S1 levels above and below. Many traders watch them, which is partly why price sometimes reacts there.

pdh.long: Yesterday's high is a common resistance level. A break above it often brings momentum buyers; a quick rejection above it is a liquidity sweep.

pdl.long: Yesterday's low is a common support level. Breaking below it often triggers stop-losses and faster selling.

gap.short: The difference between today's open and yesterday's close.
gap.long: A gap up means NIFTY opened higher, usually because of overnight global moves or news. Gaps are often partly filled during the day, but strong gaps can also extend.

smc.short: Smart money concepts: reading price structure for where big players trade.
smc.long: SMC looks at swing highs and lows, breaks of structure, fair value gaps, order blocks and liquidity sweeps. The engine measures these mechanically and tests whether they help prediction.

bos.short: Break of structure: price breaks the last swing high (uptrend) or low (downtrend).
bos.long: A BOS in the direction of the trend is read as continuation. The engine detects it on closed 5-minute bars only, so it never uses future prices.

choch.short: Change of character: the first break against the prevailing trend.
choch.long: A CHoCH can be the first sign that a trend is reversing, for example when a downtrend breaks its last lower high.

fvg.short: Fair value gap: a three-candle imbalance where price moved too fast.
fvg.long: An FVG is a price zone left untraded between the first and third candle of a fast move. Price often returns to fill part of it.

order block.short: The last opposite candle before a strong move, seen as an institutional zone.
order block.long: SMC traders expect price to react when it returns to an order block. It is a heuristic; the engine tests it rather than assuming it works.

liquidity sweep.short: A brief poke beyond an obvious high or low that quickly reverses.
liquidity sweep.long: Stops cluster above highs and below lows. A sweep takes them out and then reverses, which can mark a turning point.

heavyweights.short: The largest NIFTY constituents, such as HDFC Bank, Reliance, ICICI Bank, Infosys.
heavyweights.long: The top handful of stocks make up a large share of the index, so news about them moves NIFTY directly. The LLM flags headlines that affect them.

momentum.short: The tendency of recent moves to continue.
momentum.long: Intraday, a strong first half hour often carries into the last half hour. Momentum and mean reversion compete; the model learns which dominates in which conditions.

mean reversion.short: The tendency of stretched prices to come back toward an average.
mean reversion.long: After a large move away from TWAP or the open, prices sometimes snap back. It is the opposite force to momentum.

accuracy.short: Share of predictions whose direction was right.
accuracy.long: Accuracy alone can mislead: if NIFTY rose 53% of the time, always saying 'up' scores 53%. Compare it with the base rate and look at AUC and log-loss skill.

base rate.short: How often the outcome happens without any model (e.g. share of up moves).
base rate.long: A model is only useful if it beats the base rate. The engine reports every metric against it.

auc.short: Area under the ROC curve: how well probabilities rank ups above downs (0.5 = random).
auc.long: AUC of 0.5 is a coin flip; 1.0 is perfect. For short-horizon market direction, 0.52–0.56 out of sample is already a meaningful but small edge.

log-loss.short: A score that punishes confident wrong predictions; lower is better.
log-loss.long: Log-loss rewards probabilities that are both right and honest. The engine compares its log-loss with the base rate's; the difference is the 'skill'.

log-loss skill.short: How much lower the model's log-loss is than the base rate's.
log-loss skill.long: Positive skill means the probabilities carry information beyond 'how often does it go up'. It is usually tiny for market direction, which is normal.

calibration.short: Whether predicted probabilities match how often things actually happen.
calibration.long: A calibrated model's 60% predictions come true about 60% of the time. The engine calibrates probabilities only on earlier out-of-sample results, so they stay honest.

calibrated probability.short: A probability adjusted so it matches real-world frequencies.
calibrated probability.long: Raw model scores are often over- or under-confident. Calibration maps them to honest probabilities using past out-of-sample results.

p-value.short: Chance of seeing a result this good if the model had no real skill.
p-value.long: Small p-values (below 0.05) mean the result is unlikely to be luck. Testing many ideas raises the chance that one looks good by luck, which is why the engine also uses deflated metrics.

walk-forward.short: Testing by training only on the past and predicting the next period, repeatedly.
walk-forward.long: The model is refit as time moves forward and always predicts data it has never seen. This is the closest a backtest gets to live trading and avoids peeking into the future.

out-of-sample.short: Results on data the model was not trained on.
out-of-sample.long: Only out-of-sample results tell you how a model is likely to do live. In-sample results almost always look better than reality.

hit rate.short: Share of predictions or trades that were right.
hit rate.long: A high hit rate does not guarantee profit: many small wins can be wiped out by a few large losses. Look at average win versus average loss too.

coverage.short: Share of the time a confidence threshold is reached.
coverage.long: Raising the threshold improves hit rate but lowers coverage, so there are fewer trades. If the model reaches 80% only 0.1% of the time, rules that need 80% almost never fire.

has edge.short: The model beat the base rate out of sample with statistical significance.
has edge.long: The engine marks a model as having an edge only if its log-loss skill is positive and significant (p < 0.05). Without it, paper trading still runs but results are flagged.

edge.short: A real, repeatable advantage over chance after costs.
edge.long: In trading, an edge must survive charges, slippage and many trials. Small edges are normal; big ones are usually mistakes or leakage.

diebold-mariano.short: A test of whether one forecast is significantly better than another.
diebold-mariano.long: The engine uses it on per-day log-loss to decide whether adding a feature group really improves the model on the same days.

deflated sharpe.short: A Sharpe ratio corrected for how many strategies were tried.
deflated sharpe.long: If you test 50 variants, one will look great by luck. The deflated Sharpe ratio estimates the probability that the best result is real; the engine wants at least 0.95.

sharpe ratio.short: Average return divided by its volatility: return per unit of risk.
sharpe ratio.long: A higher Sharpe means smoother profits. Per-trade Sharpe ratios are small numbers; annualised ones above 1 are good for a single strategy.

kelly.short: A formula for the bet size that maximises long-run growth given your edge.
kelly.long: Full Kelly is very aggressive, so traders use a fraction of it. The engine uses fractional Kelly only for strategies that have passed testing.

drawdown.short: Fall from the highest equity point to the current or lowest point.
drawdown.long: Maximum drawdown is the worst peak-to-trough loss. It tells you how painful a strategy is to hold; the paper trader stops a book after a large drawdown.

equity.short: Account value: starting capital plus all realised profits and losses.
equity.long: Each paper book starts with its own ₹1,00,000. The equity curve shows how that value changed over time.

slippage.short: The gap between the price you expected and the price you actually get.
slippage.long: Fast markets and wide spreads cause slippage. The engine adds 1 point per order on top of the bid-ask spread in every backtest and paper fill.

stt.short: Securities Transaction Tax: 0.15% of the premium when you sell an option (from April 2026).
stt.long: STT is charged by the government on the sell side of option trades. Together with brokerage, exchange fees, GST and stamp duty it is included in every P&L shown here.

charges.short: All costs of a trade: brokerage, STT, exchange fees, SEBI fee, GST, stamp duty.
charges.long: A round trip on one NIFTY lot typically costs ₹60–100. Frequent trading makes charges a big part of the result.

brokerage.short: The fee your broker charges per order (often ₹20 at discount brokers).
brokerage.long: Brokerage is charged on both the buy and the sell order, plus 18% GST on it.

paper trading.short: Simulated trading with real prices and fake money.
paper trading.long: Every trade in this app is paper: no real order is ever sent. Paper trading shows how a strategy behaves live before risking money, though real fills can be slightly worse.

stop-loss.short: An exit that limits the loss on a trade.
stop-loss.long: This app's rules book exits immediately when the trade is down ₹2,000. In fast markets the actual exit can be worse than the stop level.

target.short: The profit level at which a trade is closed or reviewed.
target.long: In the rules book the target is ₹5,000. When it is reached the trade exits, unless the model gives at least 80% that the move continues, in which case it holds 30 more minutes and re-checks.

trailing stop.short: A stop that moves up as the trade gains, locking in profit.
trailing stop.long: A trailing stop follows the price at a fixed distance and never moves back. It lets winners run while protecting gains.

square off.short: Closing an open position by taking the opposite trade.
square off.long: Selling the option you bought squares off the position and realises the P&L. Most option traders square off before expiry.

mtm.short: Mark-to-market: the profit or loss of an open position at the current price.
mtm.long: MTM is unrealised until you square off. It moves with every tick.

pnl.long: For a bought option: (current premium − entry premium) × lot size × lots, minus charges once closed.

price source.short: Where a paper fill's price came from.
price source.long: broker_bid_ask means the live broker quote was used (best). broker_ltp means only the last traded price was available. model_vix means no live option price was available and the premium was estimated from India VIX.

broker_bid_ask.short: The paper fill used the live broker bid or ask price.
broker_bid_ask.long: This is the most realistic paper fill: it is the price you would actually have traded at, plus a small slippage allowance.

model_vix.short: No live option price: the premium was estimated from India VIX.
model_vix.long: Estimated premiums ignore real skew and liquidity, so P&L on these trades is approximate. Add an Upstox token to get real prices.

extension rule.short: After the ₹5,000 target, hold 30 more minutes only if the model gives ≥ 80% the move continues.
extension rule.long: The rule re-checks every 30 minutes and repeats while the probability stays at or above 80%. If the model rarely reaches 80%, the rule rarely fires and trades simply exit at the target.

against count.short: Consecutive 5-minute closes moving against the trade's direction.
against count.long: The rules book sells after 2 consecutive closes against the predicted direction while the trade is in profit, accepting whatever profit is there.

long.short: Positioned to profit if the price rises.
long.long: Buying a call is a long (bullish) position on NIFTY.

short.short: Positioned to profit if the price falls.
short.long: Buying a put is a bearish position; selling a call is also short. Selling options without a hedge can lose far more than the premium received.

bullish.long: A bullish view leads to buying calls in this app. Probabilities above 50% for 'up' are bullish.

bearish.long: A bearish view leads to buying puts in this app. Probabilities below 50% for 'up' are bearish.

books.short: Separate paper accounts, each run by one strategy.
books.long: Running strategies side by side on the same days shows which one actually works. Each book has its own ₹1,00,000 equity.

agent.short: The local LLM acting as a trader, within hard risk limits set in code.
agent.long: The agent reads the model's probabilities, news and positions and proposes an action. Code enforces the ₹2,000 stop and other limits, so the LLM can never override risk rules.

guardrail.short: A hard rule in code that overrides the agent's decision.
guardrail.long: For example the agent cannot hold a trade past the stop-loss or trade outside market hours. When a guardrail fires, the dashboard shows which one.

llm.short: Large language model: an AI that reads text, here running locally on your Mac.
llm.long: The LLM scores each headline for how it may move NIFTY and writes the pre-open brief. It runs through Ollama on your machine, so it is free and private.

bps.short: Basis points: hundredths of a percent (100 bps = 1%).
bps.long: A 10 bps move in NIFTY at 23,800 is about 24 points.

basis points.long: Small market moves are quoted in basis points. A 5 bps NIFTY move is about 12 points.

news impact.short: How NIFTY actually moved after similar headlines in the past.
news impact.long: The engine records every headline the LLM scores and the NIFTY move in the following minutes, then learns which kinds of news really moved the market and by how much.

surprise.short: How unexpected a headline is, from 0 (expected) to 1 (shock).
surprise.long: Markets react to surprises, not to news that was already expected and priced in. A scheduled event that matches forecasts usually moves little.

relevance.short: How relevant a headline is to Indian markets, from 0 to 1.
relevance.long: The LLM rates relevance so that global noise is weighted less than news about RBI, Indian macro data or NIFTY heavyweights.

magnitude.short: How big the LLM expects the market effect to be, from 0.1 (routine) to 1 (crisis).
magnitude.long: Most headlines are noise with small magnitude. Large-magnitude items are rare and matter most.

channel.short: How a piece of news reaches the market: rates, inflation, rupee, crude, flows, earnings...
channel.long: Thinking in transmission channels is how professionals judge news. For example higher crude hurts India through inflation and the rupee, because India imports most of its oil.

confidence.short: How sure the model or LLM is, from 0 to 1.
confidence.long: Confidence is not accuracy. The engine measures how often confident calls are actually right before trusting them.

fii.short: Foreign institutional investors (now FPIs): overseas funds investing in India.
fii.long: Heavy FII selling often weighs on NIFTY and the rupee; buying supports them. NSE publishes provisional FII/DII cash flows every evening.

dii.short: Domestic institutional investors: Indian mutual funds, insurers, pension funds.
dii.long: Steady SIP inflows let DIIs buy when foreigners sell, which has cushioned many NIFTY falls in recent years.

fpi.short: Foreign portfolio investors, the current SEBI term for FIIs.
fpi.long: FPI flows respond to US yields, the dollar and global risk appetite.

repo rate.short: The rate at which RBI lends to banks; India's main policy interest rate.
repo rate.long: A repo rate cut makes loans cheaper and is usually good for stocks, especially banks and rate-sensitive sectors. An unexpected hike usually hurts. The RBI MPC decides it about every two months.

rbi.short: Reserve Bank of India, the central bank.
rbi.long: The RBI sets interest rates, manages the rupee and regulates banks. Policy announcements are at 10:00 IST on decision day and can move NIFTY sharply.

mpc.short: RBI's Monetary Policy Committee, which votes on the repo rate.
mpc.long: Six members meet about every two months. Markets watch the decision, the vote split and the stance (accommodative, neutral, withdrawal of accommodation).

crr.short: Cash reserve ratio: share of deposits banks must keep with RBI.
crr.long: A CRR cut releases cash to banks to lend, which is supportive for banks and markets.

liquidity.short: How easily money is available in the banking system, or how easily an asset can be traded.
liquidity.long: RBI liquidity operations (repo or reverse repo auctions) change how much cash banks have. Tight liquidity tends to push short-term rates up.

sebi.short: Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator.
sebi.long: SEBI rules affect F&O directly, for example lot sizes, margin and weekly expiries. New restrictions on derivatives trading can move volumes and sentiment.

nse.short: National Stock Exchange of India, home of NIFTY and its options.
nse.long: NSE publishes corporate announcements, results and circulars, which are the original source for company news.

bse.short: BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange), home of the Sensex.
bse.long: Companies file announcements on both NSE and BSE. The Sensex moves almost exactly like NIFTY.

sensex.long: The Sensex and NIFTY move almost together; news reports often quote both.

cpi.short: Consumer price index: India's headline retail inflation measure.
cpi.long: Released around the 12th of each month at 16:00 IST. Inflation above RBI's 4% target makes rate cuts less likely, which tends to weigh on stocks.

inflation.short: The rate at which prices rise.
inflation.long: High inflation pushes central banks to keep rates high, which lowers the value investors place on future company profits.

wpi.short: Wholesale price index: inflation at the producer level.
wpi.long: WPI moves with commodity and fuel prices and can foreshadow retail inflation.

gdp.short: Gross domestic product: the size and growth of the economy.
gdp.long: India's quarterly GDP is released about two months after the quarter ends. Strong growth supports corporate earnings and the market.

fed.short: US Federal Reserve, the American central bank.
fed.long: Fed rate decisions move global markets, the dollar and foreign flows into India. Decisions are announced late night IST, so NIFTY reacts the next morning.

fomc.short: The Fed committee that sets US interest rates.
fomc.long: FOMC meets eight times a year. A hawkish surprise (higher rates for longer) usually hurts emerging markets like India; a dovish one helps.

hawkish.short: Leaning toward higher interest rates to fight inflation.
hawkish.long: Hawkish central bank comments usually pressure stocks and support the currency.

dovish.short: Leaning toward lower interest rates to support growth.
dovish.long: Dovish surprises usually lift stocks, especially rate-sensitive sectors like banks and real estate.

us 10y yield.short: Interest rate on 10-year US government bonds.
us 10y yield.long: Rising US yields make US bonds more attractive relative to Indian stocks and often lead to foreign selling in India.

dxy.short: US dollar index: the dollar against a basket of major currencies.
dxy.long: A strong dollar tends to weaken the rupee and pull foreign money out of emerging markets such as India.

usd/inr.short: How many rupees one US dollar buys.
usd/inr.long: A rising USD/INR means a weaker rupee, which hurts importers and foreign investors' returns but helps IT exporters.

rupee.long: A falling rupee often accompanies foreign outflows and higher oil prices, both negative for NIFTY overall, though IT and pharma exporters benefit.

brent.short: Global benchmark crude oil price, in US dollars per barrel.
brent.long: India imports most of its oil, so higher Brent raises inflation and the trade deficit and weakens the rupee: usually negative for NIFTY, positive for upstream oil companies.

crude oil.short: Oil prices, a key input cost for India.
crude oil.long: A $10 rise in crude is a meaningful headwind for India's inflation and current account. Geopolitical events in the Middle East often move crude first and Indian stocks next.

gift nifty.short: NIFTY futures traded at GIFT City, almost around the clock.
gift nifty.long: GIFT Nifty trades before NSE opens and is the best early indicator of how NIFTY will open. It is not on free data feeds, so the engine uses US index futures as a stand-in.

adr.short: American depositary receipt: an Indian company's shares traded in the US.
adr.long: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Infosys and others trade as ADRs in New York overnight. Their moves hint at how those NIFTY heavyweights will open in India.

earnings.long: Results of NIFTY heavyweights can move the whole index. Results are filed on NSE/BSE, often during or after market hours.

pre-open.short: NSE's 09:00–09:08 call auction that sets the opening price.
pre-open.long: Regular trading starts at 09:15. The engine's morning decisions use information available before about 09:10.

session.short: One trading day: 09:15 to 15:30 IST on NSE.
session.long: This app's rules book exits any open trade by 15:15, before the closing rush.

tariff.long: New tariffs on Indian exports, or global trade wars, can hurt export sectors and sentiment.

geopolitics.short: Conflicts, sanctions and diplomacy that affect markets.
geopolitics.long: Geopolitical shocks typically raise crude prices and volatility and cause foreign selling, which weighs on NIFTY.

india-relevant.short: Headlines the LLM rated with relevance ≥ 0.5 for Indian markets.
india-relevant.long: Filtering to India-relevant news removes global noise so you can focus on what is most likely to move NIFTY.
